description: 100 deep logical questions on abstraction in Python OOP

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
from abc import ABC

class Marker(ABC):
    pass

m = Marker()
print(type(m).__name__)
```
questions.answer:
Output: Marker. An ABC with no abstract methods has an empty __abstractmethods__ set, so its instances build normally.

code:
from abc import ABC

class Marker(ABC):
    pass

m = Marker()
print(type(m).__name__)  # Marker

real example:
ABCs double as plain interface markers when they declare no obligations.

Output: instantiated OK, runtime NotImplementedError, then TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class HardSub without an implementation for abstract method 'process'. NotImplementedError is a runtime convention; @abstractmethod enforces at construction.

code:
from abc import ABC

class Soft(ABC):
    def process(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

class SoftSub(Soft):
    pass

s = SoftSub()
print('instantiated OK')       # instantiated OK
s.process()                    # runtime NotImplementedError

real example:
Prefer @abstractmethod when every subclass must implement a method up front.

questions.question:
What does `@abstractmethod` do when the class does NOT use `ABC`/`ABCMeta`? Predict the output:
```python
from abc import abstractmethod

class Loose:
    @abstractmethod
    def work(self):
        return 'loose work'

l = Loose()
print(l.work())
print(getattr(Loose, '__abstractmethods__', 'missing'))
```
questions.answer:
Output: loose work then missing. Without ABCMeta, @abstractmethod is an inert flag: the class instantiates and no __abstractmethods__ attribute exists.

code:
from abc import abstractmethod

class Loose:
    @abstractmethod
    def work(self):
        return 'loose work'

l = Loose()
print(l.work())                                    # loose work
print(getattr(Loose, '__abstractmethods__', 'missing'))

real example:
Spreading @abstractmethod on a plain class gives zero enforcement and is a bug.

Output: True, True, []. register() adds Defacto to ABCMeta's virtual-subclass registry, so isinstance/issubclass pass, but no real inheritance appears in __subclasses__().

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...

class Defacto:
    def area(self):
        return 9

Shape.register(Defacto)
print(isinstance(Defacto(), Shape))            # True
print(issubclass(Defacto, Shape))              # True
print([c.__name__ for c in Shape.__subclasses__()])  # []

real example:
Third-party classes opt into an interface without touching the class hierarchy.

Output: False then True. Duck typing alone never satisfies an ABC; only real inheritance or explicit registration makes isinstance return True.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...

class Circle:
    def area(self):
        return 3.14

print(isinstance(Circle(), Shape))  # False
Shape.register(Circle)
print(isinstance(Circle(), Shape))  # True

real example:
It keeps formal interface checks honest even when methods structurally match.

questions.question:
But the *same* overwriting happens after class creation. Can you cheat at runtime by assigning afterwards? Predict the output:
```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def m(self):
        ...

class B(A):
    pass

B.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()
b = B()
print('instantiated:', b)
print('m() returns:', b.m())
```
questions.answer:
Output: instantiated: <B object at 0x...> then m() returns: None. Assigning __abstractmethods__ after class creation does take effect for the instantiation guard, but the abstract stub body still runs.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def m(self): ...

class B(A):
    pass

B.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()
b = B()
print('instantiated:', b)
print('m() returns:', b.m())

real example:
Runtime monkey-patching of abstractness is possible but fragile and never advisable.

Output: f 7. Abstractness operates on class attributes and the metaclass, never on the instance layout, so __slots__ and abstract methods coexist safely.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class S(ABC):
    __slots__ = ()
    @abstractmethod
    def f(self): ...

class Impl(S):
    __slots__ = ('x',)
    def f(self):
        return 'f'

i = Impl()
i.x = 7
print(i.f(), i.x)  # f 7

real example:
Slot-heavy records can still declare abstract contracts on their base.

Output: hi frozenset(). Abstractness is name-based only, so a shorter signature still satisfies the contract; a mismatch would only surface if actually called.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class DefSig(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def echo(self, msg, loud=False): ...

class Short(DefSig):
    def echo(self, msg):
        return msg

s = Short()
print(s.echo('hi'))  # hi
print(DefSig.__abstractmethods__)  # frozenset()

real example:
ABCs document what must exist, not the exact signature callers expect.

Output: AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute '__abstractmethods__'. Plain-type classes never gain the attribute; register() only affects checks, not abstractness data.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...

class Client:
    def area(self):
        return 12

Shape.register(Client)
# Client.__abstractmethods__  # AttributeError
print(getattr(Client, '__abstractmethods__', 'absent'))  # absent

real example:
Introspect registered classes with getattr(cls, '__abstractmethods__', frozenset()).

Output: class-attr then class-attr frozenset(). A data attribute with the right name satisfies the abstract contract, because the check is name-based.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Holder(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def data(self): ...

class Var(Holder):
    data = 'class-attr'

print(Var.__dict__['data'])
v = Var()
print(v.data, Var.__abstractmethods__)

real example:
Beware: callers doing v.data() would crash if the contract meant a callable.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
print(A.__abstractmethods__)
A()
questions.answer:
Output: frozenset({'foo'}) then TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class A without an implementation for abstract method 'foo'. ABCMeta stores abstract names in __abstractmethods__ and the object.__new__ guard rejects non-empty sets.

code:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod

class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

print(A.__abstractmethods__)
A()  # TypeError

real example:
The guard lives in the allocator, so instantiating an abstract class always fails.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
class B:
    def foo(self): return 'hi'
A.register(B)
print(isinstance(B(), A))
print(issubclass(B, A))
print(B in A.__subclasses__())
questions.answer:
Output: True / True / False. register() adds B to A's private virtual registry, so isinstance/issubclass pass while the real class graph stays untouched.

code:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod

class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

class B:
    def foo(self):
        return 'hi'

A.register(B)
print(isinstance(B(), A))  # True
print(issubclass(B, A))    # True
print(B in A.__subclasses__())  # False

real example:
Virtual subclassing changes type checks without changing MRO or inheritance.

Error: NameError: name 'A' is not defined. The class body runs while A is still being constructed, so A is not yet bound when @A.register is applied.

code:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod

class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

class B:
    def foo(self): pass

A.register(B)  # move registration after both classes exist

real example:
Register decorators must be applied only once the target ABC exists.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
class B:
    def foo(self): return 1
b = B()
print(isinstance(b, A))
A.register(B)
print(isinstance(b, A))
questions.answer:
Output: False then True. isinstance is evaluated at call time, so the same instance becomes 'an A' the moment its class is registered.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

class B:
    def foo(self):
        return 1

b = B()
print(isinstance(b, A))  # False
A.register(B)
print(isinstance(b, A))  # True

real example:
Deferred registration retroactively recognizes already-created instances.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
other = object()
def new(cls):
    return other
A.__new__ = staticmethod(new)
r = A()
print(r is other)
print(type(r))
questions.answer:
Output: True and <class 'object'>; no TypeError. The abstract guard lives inside object.__new__, so a replacement __new__ that never calls it bypasses the check.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

other = object()

def new(cls):
    return other

A.__new__ = staticmethod(new)
r = A()
print(r is other)   # True
print(type(r))      # <class 'object'>

real example:
Singleton or cached __new__ implementations can skip abstract enforcement deliberately.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABC
class A(ABC):
    def foo(self): return 1
print(type(A()))
A.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset({'foo'})
try:
    A()
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)
A.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()
print(type(A()))
questions.answer:
Output: <class '__main__.A'> then TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class A without an implementation for abstract method 'foo' then <class '__main__.A'>. __abstractmethods__ is a plain attribute consulted at instantiation, so it can be toggled at runtime.

code:
from abc import ABC

class A(ABC):
    def foo(self):
        return 1

print(type(A()))  # <class '__main__.A'>
A.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset({'foo'})
try:
    A()
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)
A.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()
print(type(A()))  # <class '__main__.A'>

real example:
Runtime toggling proves abstractness is data, not part of the class graph.

real example:
Pure interface-marker ABCs are instantiable and useful as namespaces.

Output: 'instantiated A' then 'call failed: foo()'. Raising NotImplementedError in a method body is only a runtime convention; the class constructs without error.

code:
from abc import ABC

class A:
    def foo(self):
        raise NotImplementedError('foo()')

a = A()
print('instantiated', type(a).__name__)  # instantiated A
try:
    a.foo()
except NotImplementedError as e:
    print('call failed:', e)  # call failed: foo()

real example:
Optional behavior stubs fail late; enforced interfaces fail at construction.

questions.question:
Predict the six outputs:
from collections.abc import Sequence, Mapping, Set, Hashable, Iterable
print(isinstance([], Sequence))
print(isinstance({}, Mapping))
print(isinstance(range(3), Sequence))
print(isinstance({1: 2}.keys(), Set))
print(isinstance(set(), Hashable))
print(isinstance('abc', Iterable))
questions.answer:
Output: True True True True False True. Most standard collections.abc checks pass through real inheritance; set() is neither a registered nor real subclass of Hashable.

code:
from collections.abc import Sequence, Mapping, Set, Hashable, Iterable

print(isinstance([], Sequence))            # True
print(isinstance({}, Mapping))             # True
print(isinstance(range(3), Sequence))      # True
print(isinstance({1: 2}.keys(), Set))      # True
print(isinstance(set(), Hashable))         # False
print(isinstance('abc', Iterable))         # True

real example:
Use standard ABCs for correct type checks instead of ad-hoc method sniffing.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from collections.abc import Sequence
class DuckSeq:
    def __getitem__(self, i): return i
    def __len__(self): return 0
    def __iter__(self): return iter(())
print(isinstance(DuckSeq(), Sequence))
questions.answer:
Output: False. The standard collections.abc classes no longer provide structural __subclasshook__ checks, so duck typing alone does not qualify a class.

code:
from collections.abc import Sequence

class DuckSeq:
    def __getitem__(self, i): return i
    def __len__(self): return 0
    def __iter__(self): return iter(())

print(isinstance(DuckSeq(), Sequence))  # False

real example:
Protocols are satisfied at runtime, but isinstance demands registration or inheritance.

Output: True True. Tuple isinstance returns True if any member's check succeeds; the registered A branch already passes in both orders.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

class B:
    def foo(self):
        return 1

A.register(B)
print(isinstance(B(), (A, int)))  # True
print(isinstance(B(), (int, A)))  # True

real example:
Tuple-of-type checks accept any single matching alternative by design.

Output: frozenset({'greet'}) / TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class App without an implementation for abstract method 'greet' / ok. ABCMeta unions the abstract sets of all bases; a concrete sibling method does not clear the mark unless the class itself redefines it.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Mixin(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def greet(self): pass

class Greeter(ABC):
    def greet(self): return 'world'

class Fixed(Mixin, Greeter):
    def greet(self): return 'ok'

print(Fixed.__abstractmethods__)  # frozenset()
print(Fixed().greet())            # ok
# class App(Mixin, Greeter): pass  # App() -> TypeError

real example:
Every abstract declaration must be resolved in the class's own namespace.

Output: True True True. Registering on child A2 makes B virtual for A2 and, since A2 is a real subclass of A, visible when asking about ancestor A.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

class A2(A):
    @abstractmethod
    def bar(self): pass

class B:
    pass

A2.register(B)
print(issubclass(B, A2))  # True
print(issubclass(B, A))   # True
print(isinstance(B(), A)) # True

real example:
Virtual status registered on a child surfaces on its ancestors, not descendants.

questions.question:
Predict the outputs:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
A.register(list)
print(issubclass(list, A))
print(isinstance([1, 2], A))
print(isinstance((1,), A))
print(A.__abstractmethods__)
questions.answer:
Output: True / True / False / frozenset({'foo'}). Registering a builtin type is legal, so lists become virtual A instances; unrelated tuples do not.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass

A.register(list)
print(issubclass(list, A))        # True
print(isinstance([1, 2], A))      # True
print(isinstance((1,), A))        # False
print(A.__abstractmethods__)      # frozenset({'foo'})

real example:
Adapting builtins to your interface lets isinstance accept them where suitable.

Output: TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class TopList without an implementation for abstract method 'rank' then R [0, 1, 2, 3]. ABCs mix fine with builtin bases; once implemented, list behavior stays intact.

code:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class TopList(list, ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def rank(self): pass

class Ranked(TopList):
    def rank(self):
        return 'R'

r = Ranked([3, 1, 2])
r.append(0)
print(r.rank(), sorted(r))  # R [0, 1, 2, 3]

real example:
Subclassing builtins with an abstract addition keeps performance and behavior.
